newsitem.title: USA: G7 summit not expected to dwell on Japan trade.
newsitem.headline: G7 summit not expected to dwell on Japan trade.

text.p: Leaders from the Group of Seven industrial nations are not expected to dwell at length on Japan's resurgent trade surplus at their summit later this month in Denever, G7 officials said on Monday.
"I do not expect that to be discussed in any significant way," one official, who declined to be named, said.

The June 20-22 summit will bring together the leaders of the world's top industrial democracies -- Britain, Canada, France, Germany, Italy, Japan and the United States. Russian President Boris Yeltsin will also attend much of the summit.
G7 officials said that President Clinton might raise the issue of Japan's trade surplus in bilateral talks in Denver with Japanese Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto.

But the president is not expected to be as forceful as he was when the two last met in April, when he warned Hashimoto against a big rise in Japan's surplus. "They (the United States) are softening their position," one G7 official said.

That is not too surprising. Since Clinton last met Hashimoto, the dollar has tumbled against the yen and Japan's economy has looked stronger than expected -- two developments that will restrain the rise in the Asian nation's surplus.
The dollar fell to its lowest level since November 1996 on Monday, partly on rumors that G7 leaders would focus on Japan's trade surplus at the summit.

Japanese policymakers signalled anew their concern about the steep 13 percent rise of the yen against the dollar over the last month. "Stability of currency rates ... will contribute to a self-sustainable economic recovery," Japanese Finance Minister Hiroshi Mitsuzuka said in Tokyo on Monday.
One G7 official said that Tokyo seems less concerned about the level of the dollar against the yen -- it traded as low as 111.80 yen on Monday -- than the speed of its decline.

U.S. officials, for their part, have evinced less concern recently than their Japanese counterparts about the dollar's drop, although Treasury Secretary Robert Rubin reiterated on Monday his support for a strong U.S. currency.

At their last meeting in April, G7 finance ministers agreed that currency rates should reflect fundamentals and that excess volatility of exchnage rates was not desirable. They also stressed the importance of avoiding currency rates that could lead to big trade imbalances.
G7 officials said they do not sense any great desire on the part of any of the group's members, including Japan, to change that stance significantly at the summit.
Japan's economy is looking up, and the April 1 increase in consumption taxes there seems to be turning out to be less of a drag on the economy than many had feared.
Monetary sources, who declined to be identified, said the International Monetary Fund too seems to be growing more confident about Japan's economic outlook.

The IMF, which is in the midst of its annual "Article Four" economic consultation with Japan, has forecast that the Japanese economy will grow by about 2-1/4 percent this year, although that could be revised upwards.

In its semiannual World Economic Outlook in April, the IMF urged Tokyo to keep monetary policy easy until an economic recovery was firmly established. The Fund also backed a sustained reduction in the country's budget deficit.
The IMF is expected to repeat both those prescriptions in its Article Four assessment of Japan.
The IMF has forecast a big rise in Japan's trade surplus over the next two years, but Fund officials seem much less concerned about that than some U.S. policymakers do.
